frictionVectors.title: EU Energy Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian gas while pressing Algiers on migration, pricing, and regional diplomacy. Algeria is using export access and state control of hydrocarbons to preserve strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Southern Security Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Libya, and Niger raises border-security and smuggling risks. Foreign military competition in the Sahel constrains Algeria's preference for non-intervention and regional mediation.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil still dominates export earnings and fiscal capacity, leaving Angola exposed to price volatility and declining mature-field output. International operators retain major technical and financial leverage despite efforts to expand national participation.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-for-Infrastructure Legacy
frictionVectors.details: Luanda is diversifying financing toward Western and Gulf partners, but Chinese-backed infrastructure and repayment obligations continue to shape strategic choices. The Lobito Corridor offers leverage while also increasing external competition over mineral logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence from Burkina Faso and Niger is pressing into northern Benin, forcing increased security spending and foreign cooperation. External military support is useful but creates dependency and sovereignty sensitivities.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Trade Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger remain vulnerable to border closures and political disputes, affecting transit through Cotonou. Benin is strengthening port and corridor resilience while balancing regional integration against security risks.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Market Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains substantial influence through its partnership with De Beers, but diamond demand and synthetic competition threaten fiscal stability. Negotiations over value addition and local sorting capacity are central to preserving national control.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Infrastructure Gap
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, nickel, uranium, and other minerals is rising, yet rail, power, and water constraints limit diversification. External investors will remain important, creating pressure to secure better domestic processing and revenue terms.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou is relying increasingly on Russian-linked security assistance as it reduces Western military cooperation. This may expand regime autonomy from former partners but introduces opaque contractual, operational, and political dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Control and Conflict
frictionVectors.details: The state is seeking tighter control over industrial and artisanal gold through revised licensing and national structures, while insecurity disrupts mines and transport routes. Armed groups and informal networks continue to capture value outside formal state channels.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-linked mineral networks
frictionVectors.details: Gold and coltan supply chains remain vulnerable to opaque intermediaries, weak regulation, and cross-border smuggling. Limited state capacity reduces Burundi's ability to capture full value from strategic minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Strained relations with Rwanda and reliance on regional security arrangements constrain Bujumbura's strategic autonomy. Transport and energy vulnerabilities further increase dependence on external partners.

frictionVectors.title: External competition around ports
frictionVectors.details: European, Chinese, and transatlantic actors compete for influence over port, logistics, and digital infrastructure. Praia benefits from this competition but must avoid excessive dependence on any single financier.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and limited maritime surveillance constrain Cabo Verde's control over its exclusive economic zone. Dependence on external patrol, intelligence, and fisheries agreements remains significant.

highlights: Oil and minerals remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber, and mining sectors remain shaped by foreign capital, contractors, and export markets. Weak transparency and governance limit domestic capture of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and energy influence
frictionVectors.details: Major transport and power projects depend heavily on Chinese, European, and multilateral financing. These partnerships expand capacity while creating long-term leverage through debt, procurement, and operating contracts.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-for-resources model
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security actors retain substantial influence around regime protection and extractive activity. The arrangement can improve short-term security for the government while reducing transparency and national control over mining revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Artisanal mining and border leakage
frictionVectors.details: Gold and diamond production is vulnerable to armed-group taxation, smuggling, and cross-border networks. Poor roads and limited state presence prevent Bangui from exercising effective sovereignty over many production zones.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Public finances and political stability remain highly dependent on oil exports and foreign operators. Price volatility, opaque contracting, and limited downstream capacity constrain sovereign resource control.

frictionVectors.title: External security competition
frictionVectors.details: Chad's strategic position near Libya, Sudan, and the Sahel attracts competing European, Gulf, Russian, and regional interests. Adjustments to foreign military partnerships create uncertainty around bases, logistics corridors, and regime security.

frictionVectors.title: France–Comoros Territorial Tensions
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved Mayotte dispute continues to shape migration, maritime jurisdiction, and bilateral relations. French control of Mayotte limits Comoros's effective sovereignty over nearby waters and economic assets.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence and Port Capacity
frictionVectors.details: Comoros remains heavily reliant on remittances, aid, and imported fuel, while weak port infrastructure constrains independent control of trade and fisheries.

frictionVectors.title: M23–Rwanda Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Armed conflict in the east undermines state control over territory, mining zones, and transport routes. Regional military involvement and competing mineral networks continue to internationalize the crisis.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Mineral Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Western, and regional firms remain deeply embedded in copper and cobalt extraction and logistics. New corridor initiatives may improve diversification but still leave processing and pricing power largely outside Congolese control.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil dominates exports and public revenue, leaving national resource security exposed to price swings and the bargaining power of foreign operators. Limited domestic refining and processing reduce sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure has expanded transport and urban capacity but increased dependence on external finance and contractors. Debt servicing pressures constrain the government's room to renegotiate strategic projects.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Dependence in Cocoa
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is improving farmer support and domestic processing, but foreign buyers and global commodity markets still capture much of the value from the cocoa sector.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover and Port Security
frictionVectors.details: Instability from Burkina Faso and Mali creates pressure along northern borders and raises security costs. Abidjan's port and coastal infrastructure remain strategically attractive to external investors and security partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Base and Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through foreign military bases and port concessions, but the presence of China, the United States, France, Japan, and others narrows strategic autonomy and heightens great-power competition.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Ethiopia Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy infrastructure borrowing and reliance on Ethiopian trade expose Djibouti to external debt and regional political shocks. Control over port revenues and logistics assets remains vulnerable to creditor and customer leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Suez Security
frictionVectors.details: Disruptions around the Red Sea threaten Suez Canal revenues and raise Egypt's dependence on external naval security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water Contestation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains a strategic sovereignty issue, with Egypt seeking binding safeguards for downstream water flows.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Falling or stagnant oil and gas output limits fiscal autonomy and leaves the state reliant on foreign operators, lenders, and technical expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large state-led infrastructure projects, including China-linked construction, provide strategic assets but may constrain policy flexibility through opaque financing obligations.

frictionVectors.title: Ethiopia and Assab Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Disputes over Red Sea access and the port of Assab keep Eritrea exposed to regional military escalation and diplomatic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Mining revenues and expertise depend on foreign partners, creating tension between state control, transparency concerns, and investor access.

frictionVectors.title: SACU Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Southern African Customs Union transfers and South African trade limits Eswatini's fiscal and strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Electricity, transport corridors, and access to external markets remain closely tied to South African infrastructure and regulatory conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's control over domestic power generation but continues to generate acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Finance and Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and investment needs give external creditors and partners influence over telecoms, logistics, energy, and industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: French influence recalibration
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is renegotiating longstanding French political, military, and commercial access while seeking broader partnerships. The shift increases bargaining room but could create uncertainty around investment and security cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: Commodity concentration
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on oil, manganese, and timber leaves fiscal sovereignty exposed to price cycles and foreign operators. Local-processing ambitions face infrastructure and financing constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal border and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for regional access, transport links, and security coordination. This supports stability but limits strategic autonomy over trade corridors and border policy.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and multilateral financing compete for influence in ports, roads, and energy. Debt and limited state capacity constrain Banjul's ability to capture the full value of these projects.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental stress
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal and illicit gold mining continues to damage water systems and challenge state control over mineral value chains. The government is under pressure to formalize production while avoiding disruption to livelihoods.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal stabilization and debt restructuring limit policy space even as Accra seeks greater domestic control of gold and other resources. External financing remains important for energy, infrastructure, and macroeconomic recovery.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou foreign consortium leverage
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project can transform state revenues and infrastructure, but Chinese-linked and international consortiums retain major influence over financing, logistics, and operations. Guinea's sovereignty gains depend on transparent terms and domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite exports remain dominated by foreign companies and infrastructure networks, with limited local value addition. Political uncertainty increases the risk that resource renegotiation becomes coercive rather than institutionally managed.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of cashew trade
frictionVectors.details: Cashews provide the main export income but processing and market access remain heavily dependent on external traders and financiers. This limits rural value capture and exposes the economy to price and logistics shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Political and narcotics insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Institutional weakness and recurring military-political confrontation create openings for transnational criminal networks and foreign patrons. Limited maritime and border enforcement further weakens control over strategic infrastructure and coastal resources.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure Influence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and Gulf-linked financing, alongside IMF fiscal pressure, constrains Nairobi's room to renegotiate major infrastructure and logistics commitments. The government is diversifying partnerships but remains exposed to creditor leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the Lamu corridor are contested through competing regional, Gulf, Chinese, and Western commercial interests. Security risks and uncertain demand complicate Kenya's effort to retain full strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but leave the country structurally dependent on South African infrastructure, pricing, and demand. New phases of the Highlands Water Project deepen this asymmetry.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: Large water, roads, and energy projects rely heavily on foreign lenders and contractors. Weak fiscal capacity limits Maseru's ability to capture more value or impose stronger local-content conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and other mining projects remain central to export earnings, while foreign operators retain substantial control over capital, logistics, and processing. Liberia's bargaining position is weakened by infrastructure and revenue constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Access
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors and regional actors compete for influence over port facilities, rail links, and mineral export corridors. Limited domestic capacity makes infrastructure concessions particularly consequential for sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Authorities
frictionVectors.details: Libya's divided political and security institutions leave oil production, export terminals, and revenue allocation vulnerable to factional bargaining. The National Oil Corporation remains a key national institution but operates under persistent political pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security and Energy Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Gulf states, and European actors retain influence through security partnerships, energy interests, and migration arrangements. External backing can rapidly alter control over strategic facilities and transport routes.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Value-Capture Gap
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, and other mineral projects are largely financed and operated through foreign-led structures, limiting domestic processing and fiscal capture. Commodity dependence leaves Madagascar exposed to investor pressure and price volatility.

frictionVectors.title: Land and Infrastructure Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Mining, agribusiness, and energy projects generate recurring disputes over land rights, environmental damage, and local benefits. Foreign-backed infrastructure can improve connectivity while reinforcing enclave-style development.

frictionVectors.title: External financing conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Malawi remains reliant on IMF, World Bank, and bilateral support to stabilize foreign exchange and energy imports. Debt restructuring and reform conditions constrain policy space.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic mineral governance
frictionVectors.details: New uranium, rare-earth, and niobium projects could reduce dependence on agriculture, but weak bargaining capacity and infrastructure gaps risk disproportionate foreign capture of value.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The transition authorities rely heavily on Russian military and political backing after breaking with France and regional partners. This expands regime autonomy but creates dependence on opaque security arrangements and resource-linked influence.

frictionVectors.title: Mining control and insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to increase state participation in gold mining are colliding with investor concerns, artisanal mining disputes, and attacks around production corridors. Armed groups continue to threaten transport and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas project dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers new revenue and leverage, but dependence on foreign operators, LNG infrastructure, and cross-border coordination limits immediate sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and transport concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore earnings remain tied to external demand and the state railway linking inland mines to Nouadhibou. Expansion of green-hydrogen and mineral projects could bring capital while increasing land, water, and concession pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos implementation uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius has strengthened its sovereignty position over the Chagos Archipelago, but implementation arrangements and the future of the Diego Garcia facility remain sensitive to British and American strategic priorities.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence in food and energy
frictionVectors.details: The island remains exposed to imported fuel, food, and maritime logistics, leaving it vulnerable to shipping disruptions and external price shocks despite relatively strong institutions and diversified services.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses phosphate production, fisheries, ports, and renewable projects in Western Sahara to reinforce its sovereignty claim. The strategy continues to generate legal and diplomatic friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front, and some external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital in strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, European, and other investors are supporting ports, rail, energy, and industrial projects. These partnerships strengthen Morocco's position but create exposure to competing external interests over logistics and critical supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The LNG corridor remains dependent on foreign security support and private contractors as insurgent activity continues to threaten project timelines and local legitimacy.

frictionVectors.title: Gas Revenue and Sovereign Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms retain substantial influence over project financing and operating terms, limiting near-term domestic control over gas revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Oil and Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil discoveries and uranium projects are attracting major foreign investors, creating opportunities for growth while testing Namibia's ability to secure local value addition and fiscal control.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Grid Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale hydrogen and mining plans face chronic water scarcity, limited transmission capacity, and costly infrastructure requirements.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Energy Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities are seeking greater control over uranium and hydrocarbons while relations with former Western partners have deteriorated, raising operational and export risks.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence and regional diplomatic isolation threaten oil-export infrastructure, trade corridors, and the state's ability to convert resource control into stable revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Oil Dependence and Contract Friction
frictionVectors.details: International operators remain central to upstream investment, while contract disputes, divestments, theft, and regulatory uncertainty constrain Nigeria's control over production and revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Refining Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, unreliable power, and logistics weaknesses continue to limit domestic value capture despite the expansion of local refining and industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role in regional security and mineral-trading networks remains under intense international scrutiny, exposing its export model to sanctions, reputational pressure, and diplomatic retaliation.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Investment Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign aid, security partnerships, and infrastructure investment provide important capacity but give external actors leverage over Kigali's regional policies and economic choices.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Licensing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Exploration interest in the Joint Development Zone with Nigeria creates hopes of future revenue but also exposes São Tomé and Príncipe to unequal bargaining and governance risks. Commercial discoveries remain uncertain.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on foreign partners for ports, aviation, energy, and digital connectivity, limiting its policy autonomy despite generally diversified diplomatic ties.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Energy Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas production offers Senegal greater fiscal leverage, while contracts with international operators and lenders constrain how quickly Dakar can redirect revenues toward domestic priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Coastal Security
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing, including foreign-linked fleets, remains a politically sensitive threat to artisanal livelihoods. Offshore energy infrastructure adds new maritime surveillance and environmental demands.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from tuna access agreements and foreign investment but faces persistent concerns over monitoring, value capture, and the long-term sustainability of marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: India, China, Gulf states, and Western partners compete for maritime, port, and security influence. Victoria generally preserves strategic autonomy, but its small scale creates dependence on external finance and expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects remain central to export earnings, but overseas operators retain substantial influence over capital, logistics, and technical capacity. Revenue volatility and local-content gaps limit sovereign capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining exports depend on foreign-backed ports, roads, rail, and power infrastructure, giving external investors leverage over national development priorities and regional supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Security Rivalries
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other external actors shape Somalia's port, training, and security infrastructure. These partnerships provide vital capacity but can fragment national authority and intensify disputes involving Somaliland.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Resource Governance
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, and fisheries prospects attract foreign interest while federal and regional institutions contest licensing and revenue-sharing powers. Weak enforcement leaves coastal resources vulnerable to illegal exploitation.

highlights: Electricity and logistics remain strategic vulnerabilities

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mineral value chains
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic processing and beneficiation of platinum-group metals, manganese and other critical minerals, but remains dependent on foreign capital, technology and export markets.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and freight-network constraints
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and deteriorating rail and port capacity continue to weaken sovereign control over industrial supply chains and increase exposure to external logistics and energy partners.

highlights: Oil revenues remain the state’s lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Oil transit dependence through Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan’s crude exports rely on infrastructure crossing Sudan, leaving production and public finances vulnerable to Sudan’s conflict, pipeline disruptions and bargaining by external operators.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented security and resource governance
frictionVectors.details: Political rivalries and localized armed violence constrain state oversight of oil fields and transport corridors, while foreign firms retain substantial operational influence.

highlights: War has shattered national resource governance
Ports, gold and oil corridors are contested

frictionVectors.title: Externalized control of gold networks
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and trade are increasingly tied to armed actors and foreign commercial networks, reducing fiscal transparency and allowing outside powers to gain leverage over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Port access, maritime facilities and transport corridors have become bargaining chips in the conflict, with regional and international actors seeking influence over Sudan’s coastline and export routes.

highlights: Resource nationalism is becoming more transactional

frictionVectors.title: LNG and mining investment leverage
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is using negotiations over offshore gas and major mining projects to secure greater local benefits, but large foreign investors still control capital, technology and access to export markets.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The expansion of Dar es Salaam and regional rail links strengthens Tanzania’s position, while foreign-backed infrastructure finance creates long-term exposure to external creditors and operators.

highlights: Lomé consolidates its regional logistics role

frictionVectors.title: Port-centered external influence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a major regional gateway, but its expansion and logistics ecosystem depend heavily on foreign capital, operators and trading networks, limiting domestic control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains formal ownership of phosphate resources but captures limited value beyond extraction, with technology, finance and downstream market access shaped by external partners.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: European funding and migration cooperation give the EU substantial influence over Tunisian policy. Fiscal pressure and stalled reform financing limit Tunis's room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate and energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Production disruptions and declining investment have weakened phosphate exports, while dependence on imported hydrocarbons exposes Tunisia to external price and supply shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Tilenga–EACOP project exposure
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's oil ambitions depend heavily on foreign operators, financing, and the Tanzania export corridor. Cost overruns, environmental opposition, and sanctions-related pressure could reduce national capture of future revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external lenders remain important to transport and energy development. Debt-service obligations constrain fiscal autonomy even as infrastructure capacity expands.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign dominance of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: International firms retain major influence over mines, technology, and export logistics. Zambia is seeking greater local processing and fiscal returns, but remains exposed to external capital and commodity cycles.

frictionVectors.title: Power shortages constrain mineral sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortfalls and climate variability threaten mining output and industrial growth. Reliance on regional electricity imports and emergency generation increases strategic vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors are expanding their role in lithium, platinum, and other strategic minerals. Export controls and beneficiation demands increase state leverage, but weak oversight limits domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions, currency, and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and restricted access to conventional finance push Harare toward Chinese, Russian, and regional partners. This diversification reduces dependence on Western institutions while increasing opaque debt and concession risks.
